title: Behçet's Disease: A Multisystem Vasculitis with Ophthalmic Fury
summary: Behçet's disease (BD) is an idiopathic, chronic multisystem syndrome characterized by recurrent episodes of acute inflammation, particularly aphthous oral ulcers, genital ulceration, and uveitis. With a key pathogenetic component being vasculitis, it primarily affects young adults along the 'Silk Road' route, posing a significant threat to vision due to panuveitis and retinal vasculitis. Early diagnosis and aggressive immunosuppressive therapy are crucial for managing this complex condition and preventing severe complications.

sections.title: Introduction to Behçet's Disease (BD)
sections.content: Possibly first recognized by Hippocrates, the modern description of this disease dates from the greek Adamantiades and the turk Behçet. Behçet disease (BD) is an idiopathic, chronic multisystem syndrome characterized by recurrent episodes of acute inflammation, particularly recurrent aphthous oral ulcers, genital ulceration and uveitis. The commonest ophthalmic presentation is of a sight-threatening panuveitis and retinal vasculitis.

sections.title: Epidemiology & Pathogenesis
content: **Prevalence**: Highest along the traditional Silk Route (Turkey, Middle and Far East), peaking in Turkey where up to 0.4% of the population may be affected. Lower prevalence in Europe and North America.
**Affected Population**: Typically affects young adults (peak age of onset is the third decade).

**Risk Factors**: Geographical variation including gender (reported gender prevalence varies with ethnicity), FH (more significant in Middle Eastern countries), and the HLA-B51 allele (strongly associated, more significant in Japan, with a relative risk of 6.7; ethnic groups with higher prevalence of BD also have a higher rate of HLA-B51 positivity).

**Pathogenesis**: Vasculitis is a key pathogenetic component and may involve small, medium and large veins and arteries. The condition probably has an autoimmune basis and may be precipitated by exposure to an infectious agent with subsequent cross-reaction.
**Mortality**: Around 5% at 5–10 years, typically due to cardiovascular or CNS complications.

sections.title: National Centres of Excellence (England)
content: In 2012, three National Centres of excellence were set up in England (Birmingham, Liverpool, London) to provide a multidisciplinary approach to clinical care.

sections.title: Systemic Clinical Features
content: **Oral Ulceration**: Aphthous or scarring.
**GU (Genital Ulceration)**.

**Skin Lesions**: Erythema nodosum, pseudofolliculitis, papulopustules, acneiform rash. Dermatographia (Fig. 12.27B), similar to the pathergy reaction, indicates skin hypersensitivity and consists of the formation of erythematous lines following stroking or scratching.
**Joints**: Arthritis (mono/poly) occurs in 30%, though arthralgia is more common.
**Vascular**: Thromboses (venous > arterial), including superficial thrombophlebitis, SVC/IVC obstruction. Aneurysms, including pulmonary and coronary and venous thrombosis/thrombophlebitis.
**GI**: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, bloody diarrhoea. Gastrointestinal inflammation, especially ileocecal.

**CNS**: Meningoencephalitis, sinus thrombosis ± intracranial hypertension, cranial or peripheral neuropathies, focal CNS signs. Neurological manifestations occur in 5% such as meningoencephalitis of the brainstem, dural sinus thrombosis and cerebral aneurysms.
**Hepatic and renal lesions**: Relatively uncommon.

sections.title: Ocular Clinical Features: Overview & Anterior Segment
sections.content: Ocular inflammation occurs in about 70%, tends to be more severe in men and is the presenting manifestation in about 10%. Signs are virtually always bilateral eventually. Relapsing/remitting acute onset panuveitis with retinal vasculitis and often spontaneous resolution even without treatment is the classical pattern of eye involvement. Retinal vascular disease (vasculitis and occlusion) is the main cause of visual impairment. Acute anterior non-granulomatous uveitis (AAU), often bilateral, is typical, typically with hypopyon (Fig. 12.28A). It is not granulomatous.

content.explanation: A transient mobile hypopyon in a relatively white eye (Fig. 12.28A) is characteristic of Behçet disease and JIA-associated uveitis.

sections.title: Ocular Clinical Features: Posterior Segment & Complications
content: **Vitritis**: May be severe and is universal in eyes with active posterior segment disease.

**Retinitis**: Transient superficial white infiltrates (Fig. 12.28B) that heal without scarring may be seen during acute systemic disease. There may be deeper more diffuse retinitis similar in appearance to viral inflammation. Exudative detachments can also occur. Inflammatory deposits analogous to KPs may be seen on the inferior peripheral retina.

**Retinal Vasculitis**: Arteritis as well as phlebitis, in contrast to pure venous involvement in sarcoidosis – can manifest with sheathing, perivascular haemorrhages and occlusion (Fig. 12.28C, FA showing periphlebitis (arrow heads) and arterial attenuation (arrow)). Vascular leakage may give rise to diffuse retinal oedema and CMO. This is the commonest ophthalmic presentation and is sight-threatening.
**Optic Disc Involvement**: Optic disc hyperaemia and oedema. Raised intracranial pressure can also cause optic disc swelling and optic atrophy in BD.
**Neovascularization**: Disc and retinal neovascularization may be seen as a response to inflammation and ischaemia (± vitreous haemorrhage/tRd).
**Diffuse Capillary Leakage**.
**Uncommon Manifestations**: Conjunctivitis, conjunctival ulcers, episcleritis, scleritis and ophthalmoplegia from neurological involvement.

**Complications**: Cataract, glaucoma, end-stage disease (optic atrophy, retinal atrophy with attenuated vessels (arterioles are affected later); can lead to blindness). Other complications include PS, retinal detachment and phthisis. Severe visual loss in males of up to two-thirds of patients at 10 years has been reported, but is probably much lower with aggressive management. The rate in women is about half that in men.
**End-stage disease**: Characterized by optic atrophy, retinal atrophy and gliosis and sheathing, attenuation and ghosting of affected vessels (Fig. 12.28D). The vitreous tends to clear.

sections.title: Investigations
content: There are no laboratory tests to diagnose Behçet’s disease, but there are classification criteria (see table 11.14 / ISGBD Diagnostic Criteria section).
**HLA-B51** (see above).
**Pathergy test**: Positive pathergy test – sterile pustule appearing 24–48h after oblique insertion of a 20g needle (see above).
**Inflammatory markers**: (e.g. ESR, CRP, complement levels, white cell count) may be elevated.
**Thrombophilia screening**: Appropriate in some patients to exclude other causes of thrombosis.
**Fluorescein Angiography (FA)**: Delineates ischaemic areas and aids detection of posterior segment inflammation and monitoring of disease activity.
**Laser flare photometry of the AC**: Correlates well with FA in determining the level of inflammatory activity.
**Biopsy/Aspiration**: Superficial lesion biopsy, synovial fluid aspiration and lumbar puncture may be used to help rule out alternative diagnoses.

**Systemic imaging**: May include brain MRI/MRV brain (if neurological features), magnetic resonance angiography (MRA), CT/computed tomography angiography (CTA) and conventional angiography to identify ischaemia.

sections.title: Treatment: General Principles & Agents
content: **Multidisciplinary Approach**: Liaise with physician. Refer to National Centre for advice.
**Mainstay of Treatment**: Immunosuppressants are the mainstay of treatment, but availability and expense may limit therapeutic options in many regions.
**Topical Steroids**: May be adequate if – rarely – there is no trace of posterior segment involvement.
**Systemic Corticosteroids**: e.g., initially 1–2mg/kg/d prednisolone PO; IV (e.g. pulsed methylprednisolone 1g/d IV for 3d); for an acute flare.
**Corticosteroid-Sparing Agents (Immunosuppressants)**: Consider adding these for an acute flare. Include azathioprine, ciclosporine, mycophenolate mofetil, methotrexate, tacrolimus.
**Anti-TNF Therapies**: e.g. infliximab or adalimumab.
**Interferon alfa**.

sections.title: EULAR 2008 BD Guidelines for Uveitis Management
content: **Step 1: Initial Management of Posterior Uveitis**

Systemic steroids and azathioprine (2.5 mg/kg daily) in combination are recommended. Steroids should be tapered slowly. Topical and/or regional steroids may also be used. Azathioprine may have a role in prophylaxis.
**Step 2: Management of Severe Eye Disease**

For severe eye disease (>2 lines reduction in visual acuity and/or retinal vasculitis or macular involvement): Cyclosporine (2–5 mg/kg daily) or infliximab, in combination with azathioprine and systemic steroids, is recommended.
A recent study recommended a single infliximab infusion as initial treatment of posterior uveitis.
**Step 3: Alternative for Severe Disease**

Interferon-alfa (6 million IU per day subcutaneously initially, gradually tapered) with or without steroids is a EULAR-recommended alternative to the ciclosporin/infliximab/azathioprine/steroid regimen above for severe disease.
**Step 4: American Uveitis Society Recommendation**
Infliximab or adalimumab should be considered early for vision-threatening BD.

sections.title: Important Treatment Considerations & Red Flags
content: **Ocular Hypertension with Intravitreal Steroids**: There may be a high rate of ocular hypertension with intravitreal steroid injection.

**Cyclosporine Concerns**: Hypertension, nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity are concerns. Cyclosporine should be avoided in patients with CNS involvement unless it is determined that severe eye disease warrants the risk.

**Infliximab and Tuberculosis**: Infliximab may lead to activation of tuberculosis. Screening-positive patients should receive prophylactic treatment (e.g. isoniazid). Intravitreal administration is a novel alternative route of administration for infliximab.
**Interferon-alfa and Azathioprine**: Interferon-alfa should not be used in combination with azathioprine (risk of myelosuppression).
**Anticoagulants**: Anticoagulants are not recommended.
